title: The Architecture of Academic Argument: From Claim to Conclusion

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Kim
dialogue.text: Good morning. Today I want to take a step back and talk about something fundamental: what actually happens when we make an academic argument, and what it looks like when it goes wrong. I want to use the Toulmin model of argument as a framework — it's one of the most useful tools I know for analysing and improving academic reasoning.

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Kim
dialogue.text: Stephen Toulmin was a British philosopher who, in the 1950s, proposed an analysis of how arguments actually work in practice, as opposed to how formal logic says they should work. His model has six elements: claim, grounds, warrant, backing, qualifier, and rebuttal. Let's go through them.

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Kim
dialogue.text: The "claim" is the conclusion you want to establish — the central position of your argument. The "grounds" are the facts, evidence, or data that support the claim. The "warrant" is the principle or assumption that connects the grounds to the claim — it explains why the evidence supports the conclusion. The "backing" is the support for the warrant itself — the reasons why the warrant is reliable or valid.

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Kim
dialogue.text: Interestingly, the warrant is often the weakest part of student arguments. Students typically present their claim and their evidence clearly enough, but fail to articulate the principle that connects them. "Studies show that bilingual students perform better on attention tasks" — that's grounds. "Bilingualism provides cognitive advantages" — that's the claim. But the warrant — the principle explaining why performing better on attention tasks constitutes a cognitive advantage, and why cognitive advantages matter for the claim at hand — is often left implicit.

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Kim
dialogue.text: The "qualifier" is Toulmin's recognition that most real-world arguments are not absolute — they hold in most cases, or under certain conditions, or to a certain degree. "This evidence strongly suggests…" "Under these specific conditions, it appears that…" "In the majority of cases…" These qualifiers are not weakness — they are intellectual honesty. An argument that claims too much is vulnerable; an argument that qualifies its claims appropriately is more defensible.

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Kim
dialogue.text: The "rebuttal" is the acknowledgement of conditions under which the claim would not hold — the counter-argument or exception. Notably, including a rebuttal does not weaken your argument if you handle it well. If you can identify the conditions under which your claim fails and show that those conditions do not apply in the case you're arguing, you've actually strengthened your position. You've shown that you know the limits of your argument, and that it holds within those limits.

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Kim
dialogue.text: Let me close with a practical observation. One of the most common ways academic arguments fail is at the level of the warrant — students present evidence and conclusions but do not explain the inferential step between them. The reader is left asking: "Why should I accept that this evidence establishes this conclusion?" Crucially, making this step explicit is not about dumbing down your argument for a less sophisticated reader. It is about the intellectual work of actually making the argument, rather than gesturing at it.

The principle that connects evidence (grounds) to the conclusion (claim)

vocab.definition: a counter-argument; in Toulmin's model: the conditions under which the claim would not hold
